issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette: Dr. Eduardo García is a retired dentist in his early seventies who has been widowed for several years. His life was irrevocably altered by an act of terrorism that occurred at his dental clinic two decades ago, when a group claiming allegiance to a known extremist organization stormed the building and took multiple hostages. The memory of that day remains seared into Eduardo’s mind: the sound of gunfire, the chaos, and the fear of not knowing if he would survive. Since then, Eduardo has become hypersensitive to any reminders of that event. He is particularly triggered by authority figures in uniform and conversations about military topics. These triggers have led him to engage in maladaptive strategies like self-blame and carrying a weapon for protection. Each time he hears the sound of gunfire or sees someone in a uniform, his heart races, and he becomes acutely aware of the potential threats around him. Eduardo’s memories are nonverbal and overwhelming; he can vividly relive the experience through all senses but struggles to articulate it in words. The sensory intensity is so profound that when these memories come back, they flood him with an emotional tsunami, making it impossible for him to function normally until the episode subsides. This cycle of memory recall often leads him to self-blame and further avoidance behaviors, such as avoiding news reports about similar events. The trauma has also made Eduardo vigilant in his daily life. He is constantly on high alert when he hears unexpected or loud sounds and scans for exits whenever entering a room or building. His heightened state of threat awareness influences how he perceives others; he watches people closely, looking for any signs that they might harm him. This vigilance has led to significant changes in his social interactions and daily routines. For example, when visiting the local grocery store or attending a community event, Eduardo is acutely aware of every sound and movement around him. The sight of a police car or hearing an ambulance siren can send him into a state of heightened anxiety. These triggers not only lead to self-blame but also reinforce his habit of carrying a weapon for protection, as he believes it is the only way to ensure his safety. Eduardo’s maladaptive strategies have compounded over time. The more he ruminates on what happened and blames himself for not preventing the tragedy, the more overwhelming his memories become. This further triggers his threat responses, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that makes him increasingly isolated and anxious. His occupation as a dentist has been affected by these symptoms. He avoids using certain dental tools that resemble weapons and is particularly uncomfortable when dealing with patients who have military backgrounds or uniforms. This avoidance has led to a gradual decline in the number of patients he sees, as his practice has become more challenging to manage due to his heightened anxiety. What finally brought Eduardo to seek help was a recent incident where he overreacted to a loud noise at a family gathering, causing distress for those around him. He realized that these cycles were becoming unbearable and feared they would continue to isolate him further from the world. While Eduardo is hopeful for relief from his overwhelming symptoms, what frightens him most is the fear of reliving the trauma and losing control again. Through this journey, it becomes clear that Eduardo’s triggers, memories, threat responses, and maladaptive strategies are deeply intertwined, forming a complex web of reactions that have shaped his daily life. His struggle to break free from these cycles underscores his need for support in navigating through his traumatic experiences and finding ways to reclaim his sense of safety and normalcy.
